summary: A 1971 Logger Protocol proposal by E. Meyer and T. Skinner. It was updated by RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: This proposal describes how a user at one host could connect to another host's logger and exchange login messages. It standardizes the connection and text framing while leaving each host to define its own login questions.

subtitle: A proposal for connecting a user's console to a logger on another ARPANET host.

tldr.problem: Network participants wanted a common way to log in to remote hosts instead of learning a different connection procedure for every host.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal establishes network connections using NCP control messages, then carries login dialogue as ASCII transaction blocks containing a code, a count, and characters.
tldr.outcome: The proposal covers login only; host-specific behavior after login remains outside its scope. RFC 98 was updated by RFC 123.

today: RFC 98 was updated by RFC 123, according to the unit metadata. The RFC describes a proposal and leaves post-login console communication to future work.

sections.title: Three Phases of Remote Login
sections.content:
The logger is the host mechanism that lets a user log in from a console. The RFC proposes a common network interface so each using host does not need a unique method for every serving host.

It divides login into connection, dialogue, and admission. The connection phase links the console to the remote logger. The dialogue identifies the user and checks permission. After successful dialogue, the admission phase transfers the connections to a command processor.
sections.plainLanguage: Remote login has three steps: connect to the logger, complete its login exchange, and then enter the host's command environment.

sections.title: Establishing and Closing Connections
sections.content:
The proposal follows the Initial Connection Protocol from RFC 80. The using host requests a connection from the user's receive socket to the serving host's logger contact socket. The serving host either closes the request or accepts it, closes the contact connection, and requests connections to the user's sockets.

If the user does not accept within a reasonable time, the requests are aborted. When a connection closes or a network error prevents further transfer, the logger disconnects and stops activity associated with that user. An unfinished login is abandoned; a logged-in process is stopped because the user no longer controls it.
sections.plainLanguage: The serving host accepts or refuses the connection, then opens the session's working connections. If the link fails, it ends the login or stops the user's interactive process.

sections.title: Login Dialogue and Transaction Blocks
sections.content:
Each host may choose the sequence of login questions and whether the user or logger speaks first. Messages use ASCII, with each host responsible for mapping its character set to and from ASCII. The proposed standard line ending is line feed; ESC plus another ASCII character can represent characters unavailable in ASCII.

A transaction block contains an 8-bit code, an 8-bit count, and up to 127 8-bit character elements, with the high bit zero. The code is zero for this proposal. A message may span blocks, but separate messages cannot share one block. The RFC also discusses local echo, corrections, a reasonable wait before aborting an incomplete login, and socket assignment.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts can ask different login questions, but they send answers in the same counted ASCII blocks. The count tells the receiver how many characters belong to that block.
